text.text: <atomic>The mayor of Centerville has received many letters from residents who are unhappy about traffic on the main highway.</atomic>
She assembles a team of engineers and they investigate traffic flows and come up with some possible solutions.
<atomic>The team proposes adding more lanes to the town's busy overpass.</atomic>
<atomic>The mayor says she will support the project only if it reduces commute times by at least 10 minutes and costs less than $300,000.</atomic>
<atomic>The engineers draw up a plan for the new lanes, including estimated costs of the project.</atomic>
<atomic>Then they present their plan to the mayor for approval.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>A city hires a group of engineers to build a new footbridge across a river.</atomic>
<atomic>The bridge must span the river, which is about 350 feet wide.</atomic>
The engineers develop a few possible designs for the new bridge, and they present their ideas to the city.
<atomic>City council members choose the design that provides enough space for people on bikes and on foot.</atomic>
<atomic>The engineers then create a three-dimensional model of the bridge.</atomic>
<atomic>Once this model is complete, the engineers send it to the city council for final approval before construction can begin.</atomic>

<atomic>He is working on a new house, and he needs to know which side of the roof receives the strongest sunlight.</atomic>

<atomic>Ruben finds that the panel on the south side produces far more electricity than the other panels.</atomic>
<atomic>Ruben decides he will cover the south side of the roof with solar panels.</atomic>

header.text: In April of 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human to travel into space. Just a few weeks later, on May 25, 1961, U.S. President John F. Kennedy delivered a speech to Congress that would become famous.

title.text: Kennedy Giving Historic Speech to Congress

imageLabels.text: President John F. Kennedy (center) addresses Congress on May 25, 1961.

pieces.text: In the speech, Kennedy set several space exploration goals for the United States. The effort to achieve these goals became known as
. In the following quote, Kennedy describes one of the goals of Project Apollo:

text.text: First, I believe that this nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before this decade is out, of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth. No single space project in this period will be more impressive to mankind, or more important for the long-range exploration of space; and none will be so difficult or expensive to accomplish.

contents.text: According to the quote above, which of the following statements did Kennedy believe? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Only Yuri Gagarin's flight into space would be more impressive than sending a person to the Moon.
Sending a person to the Moon would be the most challenging and costly space project of its time.
A deadline was not important for accomplishing the goal of sending a person to the Moon.
The United States should send a person safely to the Moon and back.

title.text: Kennedy Giving Historic Speech to Congress

header.text: Project Apollo put the reputation of the United States at risk.

content.text: At the time of President Kennedy's speech, the Soviet Union had launched the first satellite and sent the first person into space. The Soviet Union was overtaking the United States as the world leader in space exploration and technology.

Kennedy thought that by sending a person to the Moon before the Soviet Union did, the United States would regain its reputation as the world leader in space exploration and technology. But, by committing to Project Apollo, the United States was taking a huge risk. Failure to meet this ambitious goal would be a national embarrassment that would leave the Soviet Union as the leader in space exploration and technology.

contents.text: Project Apollo was an enormous challenge for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, or NASA. Hundreds of thousands of people from across the country needed to work together on the different parts of this challenge. They needed to figure out how to safely launch a crew from Earth, land on the Moon, and return the crew safely to Earth. To successfully complete each part of this challenge, they needed to solve many individual engineering problems.

pieces.text: To solve problems, engineers often use the

. The diagram below shows one version of the engineering-design process. In the diagram, there are six steps that engineers can work through when solving problems. Often an individual or a team will move clockwise through the steps in the diagram beginning with the step at the top (Identify the problem).

header.text: But, engineers can decide to work through the steps in any order based on the situation. They may even repeat or skip steps as needed. So, the diagram has lines that connect each step to every other step in the process. These lines represent the many possible paths that the process may follow.

contents.text: One of the first problems that Project Apollo engineers needed to solve was to figure out the best way to send astronauts to the Moon. This was a tough problem that no one had ever solved before, so several groups of engineers brainstormed ideas. While brainstorming, they had to consider several constraints, including how long it would take to design, build, and test the spacecraft, and how much it would cost.

alternativeText.text: a diagram showing the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method

elements.text: Two rockets would launch from Earth, each sending a separate section into orbit around the Earth.
While orbiting Earth, the two sections would rendezvous and dock.
A lunar mission vehicle would be put together using parts on the first two sections. The lunar mission vehicle would then be filled with fuel before detaching from the other sections.
The lunar mission vehicle would take the astronauts to the Moon, land on the surface, and then return to Earth.

elements.text: One rocket would launch from Earth, sending one spacecraft made of two sections into lunar orbit.
Once the spacecraft was in orbit around the Moon, a lunar module would detach from the other section and carry the astronauts to the Moon.
The lunar module would then launch back into lunar orbit to rendezvous and dock with the other section.
After the astronauts moved into the other section, the lunar module would detach again and crash into the Moon while the other section returned to Earth.

contents.text: One of the first problems that engineers solved was figuring out whether the Earth Orbit Rendezvous or the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous was the better method for going to the Moon. Using  information from mathematical prototypes, NASA chose the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method. The Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method would require fewer rocket launches, less fuel, and a smaller and lighter spacecraft than the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method. These advantages would allow the engineers to build the spacecraft in less time and to spend less money.

Once the decision was made to use the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method, engineers could begin designing the spacecraft and solving related problems. They could not start designing sooner because the spacecraft constraints for the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method were different than those for the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method. For example, the lunar mission vehicle for the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method would need to house the astronauts for the entire journey to the Moon and back to Earth. But the lunar module for the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method would not need to carry astronauts for that long.

contents.text: One of the first problems that Project Apollo engineers needed to solve was to figure out the best way to send astronauts to the Moon. This was a tough problem that no one had ever solved before, so several groups of engineers brainstormed ideas. While brainstorming, they had to consider several constraints, including how long it would take to design, build, and test the spacecraft, and how much it would cost.

contents.text: One of the first problems that engineers solved was figuring out whether the Earth Orbit Rendezvous or the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous was the better method for going to the Moon. Using  information from mathematical prototypes, NASA chose the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method. The Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method would require fewer rocket launches, less fuel, and a smaller and lighter spacecraft than the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method. These advantages would allow the engineers to build the spacecraft in less time and to spend less money.

Once the decision was made to use the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method, engineers could begin designing the spacecraft and solving related problems. They could not start designing sooner because the spacecraft constraints for the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method were different than those for the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method. For example, the lunar mission vehicle for the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method would need to house the astronauts for the entire journey to the Moon and back to Earth. But the lunar module for the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method would not need to carry astronauts for that long.

contents.text: One of the first problems that Project Apollo engineers needed to solve was to figure out the best way to send astronauts to the Moon. This was a tough problem that no one had ever solved before, so several groups of engineers brainstormed ideas. While brainstorming, they had to consider several constraints, including how long it would take to design, build, and test the spacecraft, and how much it would cost.

pieces.text: Engineers came up with many possible solutions to the problem. The two best solutions were called the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method and the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method. To

elements.text: Two rockets would launch from Earth, each sending a separate section into orbit around the Earth.
While orbiting Earth, the two sections would rendezvous and dock.
A lunar mission vehicle would be put together using parts on the first two sections. The lunar mission vehicle would then be filled with fuel before detaching from the other sections.
The lunar mission vehicle would take the astronauts to the Moon, land on the surface, and then return to Earth.

elements.text: One rocket would launch from Earth, sending one spacecraft made of two sections into lunar orbit.
Once the spacecraft was in orbit around the Moon, a lunar module would detach from the other section and carry the astronauts to the Moon.
The lunar module would then launch back into lunar orbit to rendezvous and dock with the other section.
After the astronauts moved into the other section, the lunar module would detach again and crash into the Moon while the other section returned to Earth.

contents.text: One of the first problems that engineers solved was figuring out whether the Earth Orbit Rendezvous or the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous was the better method for going to the Moon. Using  information from mathematical prototypes, NASA chose the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method. The Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method would require fewer rocket launches, less fuel, and a smaller and lighter spacecraft than the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method. These advantages would allow the engineers to build the spacecraft in less time and to spend less money.

Once the decision was made to use the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method, engineers could begin designing the spacecraft and solving related problems. They could not start designing sooner because the spacecraft constraints for the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method were different than those for the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method. For example, the lunar mission vehicle for the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method would need to house the astronauts for the entire journey to the Moon and back to Earth. But the lunar module for the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method would not need to carry astronauts for that long.

header.text: In April of 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human to travel into space. Just a few weeks later, on May 25, 1961, U.S. President John F. Kennedy delivered a speech to Congress that would become famous.

title.text: Kennedy Giving Historic Speech to Congress

pieces.text: In the speech, Kennedy set several space exploration goals for the United States. The effort to achieve these goals became known as
. In the following quote, Kennedy describes one of the goals of Project Apollo:

text.text: First, I believe that this nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before this decade is out, of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth. No single space project in this period will be more impressive to mankind, or more important for the long-range exploration of space; and none will be so difficult or expensive to accomplish.

header.text: Project Apollo put the reputation of the United States at risk.

content.text: At the time of President Kennedy's speech, the Soviet Union had launched the first satellite and sent the first person into space. The Soviet Union was overtaking the United States as the world leader in space exploration and technology.

Kennedy thought that by sending a person to the Moon before the Soviet Union did, the United States would regain its reputation as the world leader in space exploration and technology. But, by committing to Project Apollo, the United States was taking a huge risk. Failure to meet this ambitious goal would be a national embarrassment that would leave the Soviet Union as the leader in space exploration and technology.

contents.text: One of the first problems that engineers solved was figuring out whether the Earth Orbit Rendezvous or the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous was the better method for going to the Moon. Using  information from mathematical prototypes, NASA chose the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method. The Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method would require fewer rocket launches, less fuel, and a smaller and lighter spacecraft than the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method. These advantages would allow the engineers to build the spacecraft in less time and to spend less money.

Once the decision was made to use the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method, engineers could begin designing the spacecraft and solving related problems. They could not start designing sooner because the spacecraft constraints for the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method were different than those for the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method. For example, the lunar mission vehicle for the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method would need to house the astronauts for the entire journey to the Moon and back to Earth. But the lunar module for the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method would not need to carry astronauts for that long.

content.text: At the time of President Kennedy's speech, the Soviet Union had launched the first satellite and sent the first person into space. The Soviet Union was overtaking the United States as the world leader in space exploration and technology.

Kennedy thought that by sending a person to the Moon before the Soviet Union did, the United States would regain its reputation as the world leader in space exploration and technology. But, by committing to Project Apollo, the United States was taking a huge risk. Failure to meet this ambitious goal would be a national embarrassment that would leave the Soviet Union as the leader in space exploration and technology.

contents.text: Project Apollo was an enormous challenge for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, or NASA. Hundreds of thousands of people from across the country needed to work together on the different parts of this challenge. They needed to figure out how to safely launch a crew from Earth, land on the Moon, and return the crew safely to Earth. To successfully complete each part of this challenge, they needed to solve many individual engineering problems.

explanationText.text: Physical models and mathematical models are both prototypes. Building and testing physical prototypes is usually more expensive and takes more time than building and testing mathematical prototypes. Engineers working on Project Apollo did not have enough time or money to use physical prototypes. So, they used mathematical prototypes to evaluate the two solutions instead.

contents.text: One of the first problems that engineers solved was figuring out whether the Earth Orbit Rendezvous or the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous was the better method for going to the Moon. Using  information from mathematical prototypes, NASA chose the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method. The Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method would require fewer rocket launches, less fuel, and a smaller and lighter spacecraft than the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method. These advantages would allow the engineers to build the spacecraft in less time and to spend less money.

Once the decision was made to use the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method, engineers could begin designing the spacecraft and solving related problems. They could not start designing sooner because the spacecraft constraints for the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method were different than those for the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method. For example, the lunar mission vehicle for the Earth Orbit Rendezvous method would need to house the astronauts for the entire journey to the Moon and back to Earth. But the lunar module for the Lunar Orbit Rendezvous method would not need to carry astronauts for that long.

header.text: In April of 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human to travel into space. Just a few weeks later, on May 25, 1961, U.S. President John F. Kennedy delivered a speech to Congress that would become famous.

title.text: Kennedy Giving Historic Speech to Congress

imageLabels.text: President John F. Kennedy (center) addresses Congress on May 25, 1961.

pieces.text: In the speech, Kennedy set several space exploration goals for the United States. The effort to achieve these goals became known as
. In the following quote, Kennedy describes one of the goals of Project Apollo:

text.text: First, I believe that this nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before this decade is out, of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth. No single space project in this period will be more impressive to mankind, or more important for the long-range exploration of space; and none will be so difficult or expensive to accomplish.

contents.text: According to the information above, which of the following statements did Kennedy believe? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Sending a person to the Moon would be important for future space exploration.
It was important to send a person to the Moon before 1970.
Even though it would be challenging and expensive, the United States should send a person safely to the Moon.
All the space projects during this time period would be equally impressive to people all over the world.
